author: high
claim: Direct-plan subgoal 1 (solved): every red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on six vertices contains a monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Plan ID direct-R33. Choose any vertex v. Its five incident edges have two possible colors, so at least three have the same color: otherwise each color would occur at most twice, accounting for at most four edges. Let a,b,c be three neighbors joined to v in one common color, called color X. If one of the three edges ab, bc, ca has color X, that edge together with its two incident edges to v forms a triangle all of color X. If none has color X, then all three edges ab, bc, ca have the other color, so abc is a triangle in that other color. Thus a monochromatic triangle always occurs. author: high
claim: Direct-plan subgoal 2 (solved): there is a red-blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph on five vertices containing no monochromatic triangle.
evidence: Plan ID direct-R33. Label the five vertices 0,1,2,3,4 around a pentagon. Color the five pentagon boundary edges 01,12,23,34,40 red and color every remaining edge blue. The red edges form exactly the 5-cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0, which has no triangle: among any three vertices, if all three pairwise edges were cycle edges then each of the three would have both its cycle-neighbors inside that set, forcing those three vertices to form a connected component of the 5-cycle, impossible because the 5-cycle is connected and has two further vertices. Concretely and more simply, any three red edges forming a triangle would be a 3-cycle contained in a graph whose sole cycle has length 5. The blue edges are 02,24,41,13,30, and in the order 0-2-4-1-3-0 they also form exactly a 5-cycle, so the identical argument shows there is no blue triangle. Hence this coloring has no monochromatic triangle.
